hello.note: Reply: wa-uh-LAY-koom us-suh-LAAM. Shared with Urdu; Sikh sat sri akal is not used by Punjabi Muslims.

good_morning.note: Urdu-shared fixed greeting; GT ur confirms as the standard form. Punjabi has no distinct native 'good morning' of its own, unlike 'changi' (good).

good_evening.note: Urdu-shared fixed greeting, GT ur confirmed; mirrors good_morning's subah bakhair pattern.

goodbye.note: 'God keep you'; exact match to Omniglot's Punjabi parting phrase (rabb rakha), a Muslim-Punjabi staple heard all over Lahore.

thank_you.note: Shared with Urdu; meh-ruh-BAA-nee (mehrbani) also heard.

youre_welcome.note: 'Your welcome is'; Omniglot's phrasebook 'reply to thank you' entry (tuhada suagat hai), also GT pa/ur-confirmed. Warmer colloquial alt: 'ji sadke ji' (lit. 'I'm devoted [to you]'), attested in Western Punjabi (pnb) via Tatoeba as reply to 'you're more than welcome'.

no_problem.note: 'No matter'; Wiktionary confirms Punjabi gall = 'topic, matter of conversation' (vs Urdu baat). Shorter 'koi nahin' (lit. 'nothing') is Omniglot's reply-to-thanks form for the same sense; GT's 'koi samasya nahi' is a stiffer calque, not natural spoken Punjabi.

please.note: Literally 'by doing a kindness'; exact match to Omniglot's 'meherbani karke/karo' form, softer than formal Urdu kirpaya/baraye meherbani.

excuse_me.note: Literally 'listen a bit', informal, to get attention; Omniglot's alt for this sense is 'vekho ji/dekho ji' (lit. 'look here, sir').

sorry.note: Colloquial 'forgive me'; less formal than Urdu maaf keejiye.

yes.note: Plain and nasal; simpler than Urdu's jee haan.

no.note: Colloquially shortened to 'nai' in fast speech.

of_course.note: 'Without a doubt'; Wiktionary confirms be+shak = 'undoubtedly, without doubt', shared with Urdu. GT's 'zaroor' (surely) and 'yaqeenan' (certainly) are valid formal alts, but beshak is the everyday emphatic-agreement word.

amazing.note: 'Incredible!'; Punjabi copula ae, not Urdu hai.

delicious.note: 'Suaad' is taste/flavour; a classic Punjabi food compliment.

cheers.note: The English word; alcohol toasting is not a Muslim-Punjabi habit. Omniglot lists a native toast, 'bhag change hon' (may your luck be good), used in Sikh/Indian Punjabi contexts.
